igbo: Ọnwụ ka mma karịa ọrịa na-atịta.
english: Death is better than long sickness.
note: Read mwa as mma, kalia as karịa, and ili antitia as ọrịa na-atịta.
igbo_raw: Onwu ka mwa kalia ili antitia (As.).
english_raw: Death is better than long sickness.

igbo: Ọnwụ enweghị ọgwụ.
english: Death has no medicine.
note: Read ádênw as enweghị and jgú as ọgwụ.
igbo_raw: Qrwu ádênw jgú (As.).
english_raw: Death has no medicine.

igbo: Ọnwụ ajụghị onye.
english: Death refuses no one.
note: OCR 'Ony' ek' grwu fijt' is badly damaged; restored from the English and known proverb as Ọnwụ ajụghị onye.
igbo_raw: Ony' ek' grwu fijt (As.).
english_raw: Death refuses no one.

igbo: Okwu ụwa enweghị ụzọ abụọ; anyị ga-aga ọzọ fee anyị ike wepụ otu ụzọ.
english: The word of the world has no two roads; we should have gone to the blacksmith to sharpen an axe to shut one way.
usage: When a mourner thinks of suicide.
note: Reconstructed from a heavily damaged line; 'DEBT.' appears to be a stray category label.
igbo_raw: Okwu enu grwene mbana, rta ainyi ej' ozo fe ainyike webueie ofu yzg (Uk.).
english_raw: The word of the world has no two roads, we should have gone to the blacksmith to sharpen an axe to shut one way. When mourner thinks of suicide. DEBT.

igbo: Ọchụ anaghị agba ihe ọ na-ahụghị anya.
english: The hunter does not shoot what he does not see.
usage: A man cannot pay what he did not see.
note: Read Orhue as ọchụ and adabwa as anaghị agba; the second sentence is treated as usage.
igbo_raw: Orhue adabwa ife onafuna ainya (Ubul.).
english_raw: The hunter does not shoot what he does not see. A man cannot pay what he did not see.

igbo: Mgbe ọ bụ ọgụ, ukwu na aka tere aka.
english: When one is ready to wrestle, leg and hand are far.
usage: If a man cannot find money to buy what he needs and wants to borrow though he is a notorious debtor.
note: First half 'Ekosiem bwa' is uncertain; restored from the English and from ukwu/aka/tere.
igbo_raw: Ekosiem bwa ukwy n'aka çte (0.0.).
english_raw: When one is ready to wrestle, leg and hand are far. If a man cannot find money to buy what he needs and wants to borrow though he is a notorious debtor.

igbo: Chere m ka m tụkọ mmiri, amaghị nke chi mere ya.
english: "Wait for me to bathe" does not know what chi has done to him.
usage: A man who can wash quickly (i.e., has no sore) does not realise his good fortune.
note: Read Cem as Chere m, ntukBo mili as tụkọ mmiri, and ei menye as chi mere ya.
igbo_raw: Cem ka ntukBo mili, amwana nke ei menye (Ala).
english_raw: " Wait for me to bathe" does not know what ci has done to him. A man who can wash quickly (i.e., has no sore) does not realise his good fortune.

igbo: Ji na-adọ n'ubi, ọ lụọ ọlụ mba.
english: Yams stay in the farm and get good seed; one who lives long meets with good fortune.
note: The damaged 'olue oluamba' is uncertain; Thomas's sense is clear, but the Igbo phrase may be different.
igbo_raw: Ji nodo n'ubwo olue oluamba (Uk.).
english_raw: Yams stay in farm, they get good seed. One who lives long meets with good fortune.

igbo: Ọ bụ eme ka i daba mba ngelengele.
english: When a man uses a bad climbing rope.
note: The OCR and Thomas's fragmentary English leave this proverb unrecoverable; the Igbo is kept only as a cautious normalization of the damaged text.
igbo_raw: Mwo emekei adadi mwa ngelengele (Ubul.).
english_raw: When man uses bad climbing rope.

igbo: Nke na-akpa onye adịghị akpa ibe.
english: What troubles one does not trouble another; tastes differ.
note: Restored the OCR 'Nkg &fj' and 'àdáfy' to 'Nke na-akpa' and 'adịghị'.
igbo_raw: Nkg &fj onye àdáfy ibe (0.0.).
english_raw: What troubles one does not trouble another. Tastes differ. Uf. 408, 664.

igbo: A naghị ahọpụtara mmadụ oyi.
english: They don't choose a friend for a man; tastes differ.
note: The OCR 'Adeji aka arhainye' is difficult; I read it as 'A naghị ahọpụtara' and kept the dialect form 'oyi' for friend.
igbo_raw: Adeji aka arhainye mwady oiyi (0.0.).
english_raw: They don't choose a friend for a man. Tastes differ.

igbo: Ife onye nwe, ibe adịghị enwe; ijiji nwere akwa, ngwere na-aga ọtọ.
english: A thing one has, the other has not; a fly has cloth, a lizard goes naked; people think differently.
note: Restored 'Nzizi' as 'ijiji' and 'iigwele' as 'ngwere'; the dialect wording of the fly may differ.
igbo_raw: Ife onye nwe, ibe aderiwe Nzizi y akwa, iigwele bw' oto
english_raw: (0.0.). A thing one has, the other has not. A fly has cloth, a lizard goes naked. People think differently.

igbo: Ọgụ eju adịghị agba ọbara.
english: The combat of snails is bloodless.
usage: Used in defiance: you cannot suit me.
note: Restored the damaged 'mnie' as 'ọbara' from Thomas's meaning 'bloodless'.
igbo_raw: Ogo ejune adabwa mnie (As.).
english_raw: The combat of snails is bloodless. " You cannot suit me. DeFIANCE.

igbo: Ọkụnkọ bata n'ụlọ ọba, ọ na-ala n'oyi.
english: If a woodman goes to the head wife of Oba, he sleeps in the cold.
usage: If one man tries to injure another, it is useless.
note: The phrase rendered 'anasi oba' is uncertain; it may mean 'to Oba's house' rather than 'to the head wife of Oba'.
igbo_raw: Okbanko bwata anasi oba pla nyyi (As.).
english_raw: If woodman goes to head wife of Oba, he sleeps in the cold. If one man tries to injure another ; " it. is useless."

igbo: Akụ jee n'okwute, adịghị enwe nkọ.
english: The arrow that hits a stone is not sharp again.
usage: A doctor cannot poison a doctor; that is, you cannot harm me.
note: Restored 'adienwolo' as 'adịghị enwe nkọ' from the sense of blunting against a stone.
igbo_raw: Ako je n' okute, adienwolo (As.).
english_raw: The arrow that hits a stone is not sharp (again). A doctor cannot poison a doctor; i.e., you can't harm me.

igbo: Enyi anaghị anwụ n'ọhịa, a na-agba ya egbe.
english: An elephant does not die in the field where they shoot it.
usage: When one threatens another, the latter replies.
note: Restored the known proverb; OCR 'tinye akwy' is likely garbled 'n'ọhịa'.
igbo_raw: Enyi ádanwu tinye akwy wanabwa ebwe (Uk.).
english_raw: Elephant does not die in field they shoot him. When one threatens another, latter replies.

igbo: Otu onye abụghị ala.
english: One man is not a town.
usage: When a man disregards public opinion.
note: Standardized 'ofu' to 'otu' and 'ani' to 'ala'.
igbo_raw: Ofu onye aburg ani (Ala).
english_raw: One man is not a town. When a man disregards public opinion.

igbo: Alụsị ọcha e gbunem, gịnị ka alụsị ọjị ga-eme?
english: A white alose does not kill me; what will a black alose do?
usage: When a man disregards a big alose, he disregards a small one.
note: OCR 'Iyi' likely stands for Alụsị, and 'nem'' for gịnị ka ... ga-eme.
igbo_raw: Iyi oica eBunem, nem' iyi ofi (Ubul.).
english_raw: White alose doesn't kill me, what will black alose do? When man disregards big alose, he disregards small.

igbo: Ọ bụghị dibịa na-asa mbụda na ene.
english: It is not a doctor who washes duiker and buck.
usage: To a man who threatens to poison one.
note: Restored 'Qbuna' as 'Ọ bụghị' and 'ca' as 'na-asa'.
igbo_raw: Qbuna dibia ca mbwada ca ene (Ubul.).
english_raw: It is not a doctor that washes duiker and buck. To man who threatens to poison one.

igbo: Kịkịnta si na nwata na-achọ ihe ọ ga-eji gbuo ya, ọ na-achọ ọnụ ụzọ ebe a ga-eli ya.
english: A snake says that if a child seeks something to kill it, he seeks the edge of the street where they will bury him (the child).
usage: To a man who threatens to poison one.
note: Reconstructed from the English; 'mbumby fagente' likely 'ọnụ ụzọ ebe a ga-eli ya'.
igbo_raw: Kekenta si na rwata naey K'osi k' gbuye ya naëy mbumby fagente (Ubul.).
english_raw: A snake says if a child seeks thing to kill him, he seeks edge of street where they will bury him (child). To man who threatens to poison one.

igbo: Agwọ adịghị eje, ọ na-akwala ala.
english: A snake does not go straight away.
usage: If someone challenges, 'You cannot easily beat me.'
note: Restored 'kwalalasd' as 'ọ na-akwala ala'; the sense of 'straight away' is uncertain.
igbo_raw: Agwg adeje kwalalasd (As.).
english_raw: Snake does not go straight away. If someone challenges : "you cannot easily beat me."

igbo: Onye na-eri ihe o nwere, ihe ọ nweghị ka ọ na-achọ.
english: A man who eats what he has desires what he has not.
note: OCR 'nOU' restored as 'not'; Igbo reconstructed as a known proverb.
igbo_raw: Onye neli nkonwe nk'gninwerg &nägwßà (Ala).
english_raw: A man who eats what he has, his desire is for what he has nOU

igbo: Ọ dị n'uche onye, ma aka adịghị ezu iji mee.
english: It is in one's mind, but hands are not there to do it; if wishes were horses.
note: Restored 'adeluzie' as 'adịghị ezu iji'.
igbo_raw: Qdig' onye n'uée; mw' aka adeluzie eme (Ala).
english_raw: It is in one's mind; but hands are not there to do it. If wishes were horses.

igbo: Ọ na-eru onye nwere ndidi.
english: It reaches one who has patience.
usage: When a young man becomes by death the oldest in the idumu.
note: Thomas's 'Okul'' and 'onwß' are obscure; restored from the English as 'Ọ na-eru onye nwere ndidi'.
igbo_raw: Okul' onye onwß ndidi (0.0.).
english_raw: It reaches one who has patience. When young man becomes by death the oldest in idumu.

igbo: A naghị ebu mbu weta akalị Izoiya.
english: They don't take title earlier than Izoiya (Izoiya got yaws after taking title).
usage: To a man aiming at okpala title in youth.
note: Igbo wording is uncertain; the verb for taking title and the name Izoiya are obscure.
igbo_raw: Adawe ei mwo iwata akali Izoiya.
english_raw: They don't take title earlier than Izoiya. (Izoiya got yaws after taking title.) To a man aiming at okpala title in youth.

igbo: Onye na-akụ obere ji, na-aghọ aghụghọ onwe ya.
english: Who plants small seed yam, deceives himself.
usage: Give up designs that are too big.
note: Restored 'na-akụ obere ji' and 'aghụghọ onwe ya' from Thomas's damaged 'nepe mpeji' and 'nagg orwe alo'.
igbo_raw: Onye nepe mpeji, nagg orwe alo (Ala).
english_raw: Who plants small seed yam, deceives himself. Give up designs that are too big.

igbo: Ọbụ ibu adịghị ebu ani.
english: A carrier cannot carry the earth.
usage: To one who tries impossibilities.
note: Restored 'adịghị ebu' from 'adebu'.
igbo_raw: Obwibu adebu ani (As.).
english_raw: A carrier cannot carry the earth. To one who tries impossibilities.

igbo: Oti ukwu adịghị eti ani.
english: A fighter cannot fight the earth.
usage: To one who tries impossibilities.
note: Restored 'adịghị eti' from 'adeti'.
igbo_raw: Oti ukwu adeti ani (As.).
english_raw: A fighter cannot fight the earth. To one who tries impossibilities.

igbo: Agadi rie, okwele ọgụ.
english: An old man eats, he agrees to fight.
usage: A man is induced to risk his life when he has something to gain.
note: Onitsha 'lie' restored to standard 'rie'.
igbo_raw: Agadi lie, okwel' ggo (0.0.).
english_raw: Old man eats, he agrees to fight. A man is induced to risk his life when he has something to gain.

igbo: Mbeku adịghị arị ukpo.
english: A tortoise cannot climb a throne (ukpo).
usage: When a man tries something beyond him.
note: Thomas's 'adali' and 'okbo' are read as 'adịghị arị ukpo'; the trailing 'EXpErIence' tag is unclear.
igbo_raw: Mbeku adali okbo (As.).
english_raw: A tortoise cannot climb a throne (ukb'o). When a man tries something beyond him. EXpErIence.

igbo: Anyị ahụgo nnụ mmadụ, anyị adịghị akpọzi ọgọ mmadụ ihe.
english: We see four hundred men, we do not call two hundred men anything.
usage: One does not go out to see a smaller thing than one has already seen.
note: Restored the numerals nnụ (400) and ọgọ (200); Ika 'ife' normalized to standard 'ihe'.
igbo_raw: Ainyi afugo nno mwadu, ainyi adakpozi ogo mwad' ili
english_raw: ife (I.A.). We see four hundred men, we do not call two hundred men anything. One does not go out to see a smaller thing than one has already seen.

igbo: Mbụ m onye; ọdị abụọ m mara ihe.
english: First (thing) does one; the second (time) he knows it.
usage: A man learns by experience.
note: OCR '0.0.' read as O.O.; 'mwal'' restored as mara.
igbo_raw: Mby m'onye; owd abg mwal' ife (0.0.).
english_raw: First (thing) does one; the second (time) he knows it. A man learns by experience.

igbo: Onye jere aka, ọ hụrụ aka.
english: Who walks far, sees much.
note: Thomas's 'jeluka/qfuluka' read as jere aka / hụrụ aka.
igbo_raw: Onye jeluka, qfuluka (As.).
english_raw: Who walks far, sees much.

igbo: Ibebune nwa Nwọmọ sị n'etukwa ani kụọ ọkpụ, na-ele onwe ya anya; ọ ka mma karịa onye kwụ ọtọ.
english: Ibebune, son of Nwomo, says that who stoops and beats drum observes himself; he beats better than one who stands.
usage: People observe what their fellows do.
note: The proverb is split across the OCR lines; the second half is reconstructed from Thomas's English and remains uncertain.
igbo_raw: Ibebune riwa Nwomg si n' etukw ani kbg okarga iyime
english_raw: onwe ainya; okhonarhina onye ku pte (I.A.). Ibebune, son of Nwomo, says that who stoops and beats drum observes himself; he beats better than one who stands. People observe what their fellows do.

igbo: Ụwa nke a anyị bịara, ha adịghị eji enwe lie adaka.
english: This world we come to, they never take enwe to bury adaka.
usage: When monolinguals of different tongues meet, they don't kill each other.
note: OCR 'Uhwe aud adaka' restored as enwe and adaka; 'puta' read as bịara.
igbo_raw: Owa nka ainyi puta wa' adeji zi giwe eni adaka (Uk.).
english_raw: This world we come to, they never take enwe to bury adaka. When monolinguals of different tongues meet, they don't kill each other. Uhwe aud adaka are species ot monkey.

igbo: Ọfịa asị akpa ya epụne elo.
english: If a bush forbids bag, it must not grow fungus.
usage: One who does not wish to be abused, does not abuse. (Do as you would be done by.)
note: The proverb's exact wording is uncertain; 'asp' and 'epune' are read as asị and epụne.
igbo_raw: Ofia asp akBa ya epune elo (Uk.).
english_raw: If a bush forbids bag, it must not grow fungus. One who does not wish to be abused, does not abuse. (Do as you would be done by.)

igbo: Ndị anya mkpị abụọ zutere n'ụzọ, otu anya aka ekpe, otu anya aka nri.
english: Two half blind men meet by the way, one no left eye, one no right eye.
usage: Don't ask others to do what you won't do yourself.
note: OCR heavily damaged; the second half is reconstructed from the English and remains uncertain.
igbo_raw: Ndi ainyampi nabp zu n' y20, ofu ainy' gro ibakekbe ofu ainy' oro n' ibakanni (Ubul.).
english_raw: Two half blind men meet by the way, one no left eye, one no right eye. Don't ask others to do what you won't do yourself.

igbo: Aka nri kwọ aka ekpe; aka ekpe akwọ aka nri.
english: The right hand washes the left and the left washes the right.
usage: Of mutual respect.
note: OCR 'Akanne' read as aka nri; 'akanni' as aka nri.
igbo_raw: Akanne kwo akekpe; akekpe akwo akanni (As.).
english_raw: The right hand washes the left and ayenward. Of mutual respect.

igbo: Ajụ abụọ eji ebu aga, eji ebu ọmụnwa; ọmụnwa adịghị aga n'ajụ.
english: Two head pads carry sterile woman, they carry a fruitful woman; fruitful woman does not pass sterile with pad.
usage: When fruitful woman boasts to sterile woman, two men carry her when she dies, whether she has children or not.
note: The proverb's exact wording is uncertain; 'aga' is read as the barren woman and 'ọmụnwa' as the fruitful woman.
igbo_raw: Aju nabo gjibu' aga k'eji bu gmunwa ; omunwa adiak' aga n'aju (As.).
english_raw: Two head pads carry sterile woman, they carry a fruitful woman; fruitful woman does not pass sterile with pad. When fruitful woman boasts to sterile woman, two men carry her when she dies, whether she has children or not.

igbo: Anị naa amazu, k'ego aka mwa ha abụghị imalegwe.
english: The whole country does not meet and tie cowries while they are not imalegwe.
usage: When two meet and quarrel, one boasts of his cowry wristlet.
note: The OCR and dialect forms leave much of the proverb uncertain, especially amazu and imalegwe.
igbo_raw: Ani nãa amazu K' ego aka mwa fa abuna imalegwe
english_raw: (I.A.). The whole country does not meet and tie cowries while they are not imalegwe. When two meet and quarrel; one boasts of his cowry wristlet.

igbo: Ọkọkọ sị kpọmpana, ọ bụrụ na ọ na-aga ilo ya, ya loo ya ozugbo, ya na-eme ya amụma ọjọọ, ajụ nye ya n'anya.
english: Fowl says to butterfly, if he is going to swallow him, swallow him at once, let him not wilfully make him giddy.
usage: No answer to repeated threats.
note: Heavily OCR-damaged; the second half of the proverb is only partly recoverable.
igbo_raw: Okoko si kpankpana, obuly nojege nuye, ya nuege na ya amwan(a) omwa èu aju nyeya n'ainga (Ala).
english_raw: Fowl says to butterfly, if he is going to swallow him, swallow him at once, let him not wilfully make him giddy. No answer to repeated threats.

igbo: Oke bwagoro je n'elu nkwụ, ọ sị ozi ziri enyi; ya na-akwụ okpete n'anya, ga-eje akwụ ọmụ.
english: The rat runs up oil palms, says he sends messenger to elephant, let him root out sugar cane, that he goes to root out young palm leaves.
note: The first word and final clauses are uncertain; the OCR forms Ogini and gmu are not clearly recoverable.
igbo_raw: Ogini bwago je enynkwy qsi ozinzi zienyi; ya nekwu pkbete naiya geje ckwu gmu (Ala).
english_raw: The rat runs up oil palms, says he sends messenger to elephant, let him root out sugar cane, that he goes to root out young palm leaves.

igbo: Otu mkpụrụ akọ adịghị efu n'ọkụ.
english: One nut is not lost in the fire.
usage: Of a boaster.
note: Thomas's ikpulako is normalized to mkpụrụ akọ; a dialect spelling ikpụrụ akọ is also possible.
igbo_raw: Ofu ikpulako adiefq n' pky (As.).
english_raw: One nut is not lost in the fire. Of boaster.

igbo: Ọ dịghị ije mmụọ.
english: You cannot walk to the other world.
usage: To a boaster.
igbo_raw: Ojtje Jê mwg (As.).
english_raw: You cannot walk to the other world. To boaster.

igbo: Ka onye kwụ ka ọdị ya; ka adakada jila nwunye ngwere kwụ ụkpọ ego.
english: Let one pay according to one's size; dung beetle cohabits with lizard's wife and pays one cowry fine.
usage: To a boaster.
note: The OCR rha and iikpplego are normalized as kwụ and ụkpọ ego with some uncertainty.
igbo_raw: K' onye rha k' odà ya k' adakada ji la nwunye ngwele rha iikpplego (Ubul.).
english_raw: Let one pay according to one's size; dung beetle cohabits with lizard's wife and pays one cowry fine. To boaster.

igbo: Ọkwa egwu adịghị emeri ngwesi.
english: A dancer does not dance better than ngwesi (yellow wagtail).
usage: To a boaster.
note: Thomas's adetenerhi is read as adịghị emeri; ngwesi is kept as the bird name.
igbo_raw: Okegwu adetenerhi ngwesi (0.0.).
english_raw: A dancer does not dance better than ngwesi (yellow wagtail). To boaster.

igbo: Ọ dịghị iwe dịka onye anwụrụ anwụ.
english: They do not feel cross more than one who has smoke in his face.
usage: Two rich men boasting.
note: The OCR Wadebu iru aka and eme are obscure; the reading follows the English sense.
igbo_raw: Wadebu iru aka onye anwulu eme (Ubul.).
english_raw: They don't feel cross more than one who has smoke (in his face). Two rich men boasting.

igbo: Anụ m na-afa na-eyi aja otu obwe, ma nke obwe na-abọ amaghị m.
english: I hear they make sacrifice for bad travelling, but for coming back I don't know.
usage: One thing at a time (?); refusal to fall in with a suggestion.
note: Thomas notes that 'ofu obwe' is diviner's language; the Igbo is largely reconstructed from his phonetic spellings.
igbo_raw: Anum nafa naëy aja ofu obwe, mwa nke obwe nabo amwozinam (Ubul.).
english_raw: I hear they make sacrifice for bad travelling, but for coming back I don't know. One thing at a time (?) Refusal to fall in with suggestion. Ofu obwe is diviner's language.

igbo: Efi sị na ọ masị ya iso ndị ahịa ije; ọ daa, ndị ahịa agaghị ebu ya.
english: The cow says it pleases her to walk with traders; if she falls the traders will not carry her.
usage: Refusal to accompany messenger.
note: The middle of Thomas's line is badly OCR-damaged; the Igbo follows the English meaning rather than a secure phonetic reading.
igbo_raw: Efi si na osoiya osg cjenye qkene ije naiya da pleng amabuye (Ubul.).
english_raw: The cow says it pleases her to walk with traders; if she falls the traders will not carry her. Refusal to accompany messenger.

igbo: A dajụ onye ka ọ sị kọ ntọ ya.
english: They don't ask one how he scratches his sore.
usage: A man who refuses to cease at bidding.
note: 'dajụ' is kept as Thomas's dialect form; modern standard might use 'ajụ'.
igbo_raw: Wadaju onye k' osi kg ntoa (Ubul.).
english_raw: They don't ask one how he scratches his sore. A man who refuses to cease at bidding.

igbo: Owu dị n'isi ka oke jiri aha ọmangana.
english: Fame is on the head as the rat takes the name of omangana (one who sits in one place).
usage: If a lame man, e.g., is successful.
note: Thomas's 'K'eyi jille omangâna' is restored as 'ka oke jiri aha ọmangana' following the English.
igbo_raw: Owu dj n'isi K'eyi jille omangâna (As.).
english_raw: Fame is on the head as rat takes name of gmangana (one who sits in one place). If lame man, e.g., is successful.

igbo: Ọgọli dị n'udo n'ihi na ọ bụ naanị ya n'ụlọ di ya.
english: A woman is quiet because she alone is in husband's house.
usage: People interfere only with successful man.
note: The Igbo restoration is provisional; Thomas's compressed spelling does not securely yield each word.
igbo_raw: Ogoli d'Odò naiyasi ngnibe diye (Ala).
english_raw: A woman is quiet because she alone is in husband's house. People interfere only with successful man,

igbo: Nkịtị ọsa gbụrụ akwụ, ọsa a sara ike pịju ọdọdọ.
english: Ever since the squirrel cut nuts it has never been able to fill calabash with oil.
usage: Of an unsuccessful man who works hard.
note: 'Nkịtị' and 'a sara' are uncertain; the proverb is reconstructed from the English and Thomas's garbled consonants.
igbo_raw: Nkiti qsa Bume akwu, qsa ásana ike piju фdodo (Ubul.).
english_raw: Ever since the squirrel cut nuts it has never been able to fill calabash with oil. Of an unsuccessful man who works hard.

igbo: Ọ dị mma inye enwe mmanya, ma onye ga-eweta ọkwa?
english: It is fitting to give palm wine to a monkey; but who will bring the calabash back?
usage: When a farmer sees he succeeds less than a man who planted less.
note: 'ọkwa' is restored as the calabash from Thomas's 'dbwd'; 'ma onye' may also be read 'mana onye'.
igbo_raw: Ainya adigo kainye grwe mwainya, onebo onye ganata eiwe dbwd (As.).
english_raw: It is fitting to give palm wine to a monkey; but who will bring the calabash back? When a farmer sees he succeeds less than a man who planted less.

igbo: Ọ na-eme m n'amaghị m; ma m maara, gịnị ka m ga-eme?
english: He troubles me because I did not know; if I had known what should I have done?
usage: Unsuccessful man tries various plans.
note: Thomas's 'amwanam' is restored as 'amaghị m' and 'mwale' as 'maara'.
igbo_raw: Omem n' amwanam; mwa mwale gini kangeme (0.0.).
english_raw: He troubles me because I did not know; if I had known what should I have done ? Unsuccessful man tries various plans.

igbo: Ọtọntọ adaghị ọkọ isi.
english: A trickster cannot trick the barber.
usage: To a boastful trickster.
note: Restored 'Ọtọntọ adaghị ọkọ isi' from OCR 'Qtonto adato gko isi'.
igbo_raw: Qtonto adato gko isi (As.).
english_raw: A trickster cannot trick the barber. To boastful trickster.

igbo: Akpata sị na ya na-ekwu okwu na nnụ na mwa, onye nwe ya amaghị.
english: The guitar says that it speaks 20 and 400, but its owner does not know.
usage: Used in a quarrel when a young man boasts of his progress.
note: Restored 'sị na ya na-ekwu okwu' and the owner phrase; the numerals 'nnụ na mwa' remain uncertain.
igbo_raw: Akbata si n' aiya n' ekwu orhu na nnq mwa dinweniye adamwa (As.).
english_raw: The guitar says that he speaks 20 and 400, but his owner does not know. In a quarrel when a young man boasts of his progress.

igbo: Onye amala adịghị apị n'apịtị.
english: The paddler does not paddle in the mud.
usage: Of one who talks of himself against another; one leg does not stand up. If two men begin a title and only one finishes and boasts, the other replies, 'You had backers.'
note: Restored 'adịghị apị n'apịtị' from OCR 'adainya n' ply'.
igbo_raw: Ony' âmala adainya n' ply (As.).
english_raw: The paddler does not paddle in the mud. Of one who talks of self " against another." One leg does not stand up. If two men begin title and only one finishes and boasts, other replies, you had backers.

igbo: Nnụnụ adịghị efe nke ọbụna, nwa Ako.
english: A bird does not fly like an egret, child of Ako.
usage: To a boaster: he cannot be richer than the king.
note: Uncertain 'ọbụna' and 'Ako'; restored from the English and OCR 'obwana Ako'.
igbo_raw: Nnono adefe nke obwana Ako (0.0.).
english_raw: Bird does not fly as egret, child of Ako. To boaster-cannot be richer than king.

igbo: Otu onye adịghị eguzo n'ụzọ abụọ.
english: One man does not stand in two roads.
usage: To a man who boasts of many children (it takes a woman also).
note: Restored 'eguzo' for dialect 'ezo' and 'n'ụzọ abụọ' from OCR 'n' yzg nabg'.
igbo_raw: Ofu onye adew' yzo n' yzg nabg (0.0.).
english_raw: One man does not stand in two roads. To a man who boasts of many children (it takes woman also).

igbo: Osisi ọ dịghị ka onwala mma.
english: No tree is finer than onwala.
usage: To a boaster who has no wife or child.
note: Restored 'ọ dịghị ka' from OCR 'odaka'; the plant name 'onwala' is uncertain.
igbo_raw: Osisi odaka onwala mma (0.0.).
english_raw: No tree is finer than onwala. To boaster who has no wife or child.

igbo: Anyanwụ ụtụtụ akaghị akwa; nke anyasị bụ abwọlọ.
english: The morning sun does not dry clothes; the evening sun is weak (not strong enough to dry).
usage: When a man who has not worked at all boasts of when he will finish.
note: Restored 'anyasị' from OCR 'ainyase'; 'akaghị akwa' is uncertain.
igbo_raw: Ainyanwu Stòtò akgn' äkwä; nk' ainyase bu abwolo
english_raw: (0.0.). The sun of the morning does not dry clothes; the evening sun is weak (not strong enough to dry). When a man who has not worked at all boasts of when he will finish.

igbo: Agụ bụ onye ọma, gbazụ bụ onye ọma, agụ gbuo gbazụ bụ gbazụ nkịli.
english: The leopard is a good creature, and the guinea fowl is too; the leopard kills the guinea fowl and keeps looking at it.
usage: When rivals try to eclipse each other and spoil each other's show.
note: Restored from OCR; 'nkịli' is uncertain.
igbo_raw: Ágo bp ony' pma, ggazu by ony' oma, ago çbu ggazu bu ggazu nkili (Ala).
english_raw: The leopard is a good creature, the guinea fowl is too; the leopard kills the guinea fowl and keeps looking at it. When rivals try to eclipse each other and spoil each other's show.

igbo: Onye Agolo sị eyi: ebwana gbaa, ọ bụ mụ na gị n'ala Agolo; ebwana gbaga, ọ bụ mụ na gị n'ala Agolo.
english: If you do not run, it is you and me in Agolo.
usage: If two boasters meet, 'wait till year comes.'
note: OCR and transcription are badly damaged; the repeated 'rhia/rhirhga' is read uncertainly as gbaa/gbaga, and 'ani' has been normalized to ala.
igbo_raw: Onye Agolo si eyi: ebwanarhia obu ngina (? mu) n'ani Agolo; ebwana rhirhga, obu ngina (mu) n'ani Agolo (As.).
english_raw: and me in town of Agolo; if you do not run, it is you and me in Agolo. If two boasters meet, "wait till year comes."

igbo: Nkịta amaghị eteta ụla, zịzịpụ ntụ; ebe ọ maghị ute, anyasị alaghachikwa na ntụ.
english: The dog does not wake in the morning and shake off the ashes; but if it does not order a mat, in the evening it sleeps in the ashes again.
usage: Of idle boasting of a man who has done nothing.
note: Restored ụla, ntụ and anyasị; 'Stoto' is left unread as likely OCR garble.
igbo_raw: Nkite amateta ola Stoto zizipu nto; ebe omatorò ute, ainyase alarokwa na nto (Uk.).
english_raw: Dog does not wake in morning and shake off ashes; but if it does not order mat, in the evening it sleeps in the ashes again. Of idle boasting of man who has done nothing.

igbo: Onye n'uche, onye n'uche.
english: Who has his opinion, has his opinion.
usage: To obstinate man.
note: OCR ü and tone marks normalized to standard uche.
igbo_raw: Onyê n'üce, ónyê n'ücê (0.0.).
english_raw: Who has his opinion, has his opinion. To obstinate man.

igbo: Mba, e wem aka, ndụ pịa onye aka.
english: I cannot crush my hand because of insects.
usage: Refusal.
note: The transcribed words are uncertain, especially ndụ/insects and the final phrase.
igbo_raw: Mwa we mw' aka ndu pia ony aka (Ubul.).
english_raw: I can't crush my hand because of insects. Refusal.

igbo: K'ị ma aka ihe, ị ma gọ ijiji ụnyaahụ?
english: As you know a thing, did you know the fly of yesterday?
usage: Used especially by women; if a woman refuses, e.g., salt to one from whom she borrows often.
note: OCR damaged; 'benyà' may be banyere or a dialect form for yesterday.
igbo_raw: K'imwak' ife, imwago ijiji benyà (0.0.).
english_raw: As you know a thing, did you know the fly of yesterday (used especially by women). If woman refuses, e.g., salt to one from whom she borrows often.

igbo: Ọgọli mụaka, ọ danyeghị onwe.
english: A woman is fine, she does not marry herself.
usage: Girl who refuses suitors.
note: Transcription is uncertain; 'Ogoli' may be ọgọli and the negative may be ọ danye onwe as printed.
igbo_raw: Ogoli 'mwaká, qdany onwê (Alá).
english_raw: Woman is fine, does not marry herself. Girl who refuses suitors.

igbo: Ọchụta amụghị mgbada, atawo aka; n'ụtụtụ echi ọ ga-ahụ ya.
english: A hunter misses a duiker, bites his finger; at dawn next day he will see it.
usage: When a man's request is refused.
note: OCR is badly damaged; the second half is reconstructed from the English sense.
igbo_raw: Orhte amw'afie mbwada, atabe aka; mwa cify niya gafy (Uk.).
english_raw: A hunter misses duiker, bites finger; at dawn next day he will see it. When man's request is refused.

igbo: Ọsa sị enunokwu zịdete, sị plili gaa kpanye ekwele.
english: Squirrel comes down from palm and says to ground squirrel: go and get me cord (from tree).
usage: Refusal to do what is requested.
note: Restored zịdete and gaa kpanye; 'enunkwu' read as enunokwu.
igbo_raw: Qsá si enunkwu zidete, si plili gekbenye ekwele (Ubul.).
english_raw: Squirrel comes down from palm says to ground squirrel: go and get me cord (from tree). Refusal to do what is requested.

igbo: Ọ dịghị ịkọbi esi ọkwa ma mmiri ngọ adịghị na ya.
english: One can try hard for riches, but fail if it is not his lot.
note: Restored Wadeji as Ọ dịghị and mili as mmiri; ịkọbi's sense uncertain.
igbo_raw: Wadeji ikobi esi okwa mwa mili ngo ádjna (I,A.).
english_raw: They never try hard to cook okwa if water of ngo (lye) is not in it. One can try hard for riches, but fail if it is not his lot.

igbo: Mmiri ọbụwa ji awọ ahụ, ka ugo ji ncha ịsa ahụ; nke ugo abara ugo n'ife.
english: One's labour is useless, another's fruitful.
note: nife is uncertain; ọbụwa and awọ are probable but damaged.
igbo_raw: Mili obwana ji wy ary k'ugo jinyaica ary; nk'ugo abal'ugo nife (As.).
english_raw: Water egret takes wash body, is the same that cagle takes wash (with soap) body ; ugo's water is gain for him. One's labour is useless, another's fruitful.

igbo: Ọ tẹ anya bịa n'isi.
english: It is long when the eye comes to the head.
usage: Of long and fruitless discussion; postponement.
note: tẹ may be tọ; OCR ambiguous.
igbo_raw: Óté ainya bia n'isi (0.0.).
english_raw: It is long when the eye comes to the head. Of long and fruitless discussion- postponement.

igbo: Hapụ ebwe, kwebe n'ebe ọ kwụtị.
english: Leave ebwe (tree), let it stand where it stands.
usage: Postponing action (if one is in trouble).
note: Yalo restored as Hapụ; pkuti as kwụtị.
igbo_raw: Yalo ebwe kebwe w'ebe pkuti (Ubul.).
english_raw: Leave ebwe (tree), let it stand where it stands. Postponing action (if one is in trouble).

igbo: Ụzọ dị owu, nduru eburu akpa.
english: Road is cool, dove takes up bag.
usage: To an unwelcome or inconvenient visitor; 'come another time,' when a man has other business and postpones a caller.
note: nduli restored as nduru; ekol' as eburu.
igbo_raw: UzQ d'owu, nduli ekol' akba (As.).
english_raw: Road is cool, dove takes up bag. To unwelcome or inconvenient visitor; " come another time," when man has other business and postpones caller.

igbo: Ụsụ si nne n'ime afọ, ọ ga-amụ ya, ya amụnye n'afọ.
english: Bat tells mother while in womb, if she delays to deliver her, she will bear her own child in womb.
usage: To procrastinator.
note: OCR badly damaged; reconstruction uncertain.
igbo_raw: Osq si nne n'im'oka gamyya, yamunye n'afg (As.).
english_raw: Bat tells mother while in womb, if she delays to deliver her, she will bear her own child in womb. To procrastinator.

igbo: Ọnwụ dịkebe nwa ọkete, ọ ga-eto ka nne nkwụ.
english: Children will grow up.
note: dịkebe and ọkete are uncertain; nnenkwu read as nne nkwụ.
igbo_raw: Onwu dikeBu nw' okete, ogelugo ka nnenkwu (Ala).
english_raw: If the young oil palm does not die, it will grow big. Children will grow up.

igbo: Okenye tosie, ọ cịa ibe.
english: A child may be ill-treated but not a man.
note: sosie read as tosie; cịa uncertain.
igbo_raw: Okenye sosie, ocg ibe (0.0.).
english_raw: When a man stops growing, he waits for his fellows. A child may be ill-treated but not a man.

igbo: Lege lege bụ m udụ; mkpịsị aka nwata adabaghị n'anya eje.
english: A child talks nonsense: a child's finger does not go through the eye of a bead.
usage: A child cannot abuse a grown person.
note: Restored mkpịsị aka and eje; the first phrase remains uncertain.
igbo_raw: Lége lege bwam udü : (reply) nkpesiaka rwata adaba n'ainya ejije (As.).
english_raw: A child talks nonsense: a child's finger does not go through the eye of a bead. A child cannot abuse a grown person.

igbo: Nwata adịghị egwu Nkpetime.
english: A child does not swim Nkpetime (pond).
usage: A child must pay attention.
note: OCR 'adegu' read as adịghị egwu; Nkpetime kept as a pond name.
igbo_raw: Nwata adegu Nkpetime (0.0.).
english_raw: A child does not swim Nkpetime (pond). A child must pay attention.

igbo: Okwu bụ ọkpọlọ, ebe a tụlonye ya, mbia osi.
english: A word is hard clay; where they throw it, it goes.
usage: A child and a big man do not know the same things.
note: Final words 'mbia osi' are uncertain; ọkpọlọ restored for hard clay.
igbo_raw: Okwu bu okpolo, eb' atolonye, mbia osi (As.).
english_raw: A word is hard clay, where they throw it, it goes. A child and a big man do not know the same things.

igbo: Nwata gara njem maara ihe karịa oke nọ n'ụlọ.
english: A travelled child knows better than the old man who sits at home.
usage: If a young man's advice is refused, when he has learnt from his father.
note: OCR 'oku njenje' read as gara njem; Thomas's usage note is garbled.
igbo_raw: Nwatà oku njenje namwa ife akali okei n'ung (Ala).
english_raw: A travelled child knows better than the old man who sits at home. If young man's advice is refused, when he has learnt from father.

igbo: Onye na-anụghị ihe, ọnwụ bụ enyi ya.
english: One who cannot hear, death is his companion.
usage: When young men refuse the advice of an older man.
note: Thomas's transcription is badly garbled; restored to the known proverb.
igbo_raw: Anuany n'onwiye (As.).
english_raw: One who can't hear, death is his companion. When young men refuse the advice of an older man.

igbo: Ịhụ ngkụ na-egbu oke; ekwu na-anụ na-egbu ikolo.
english: Seeing and keeping silence kills an old man; speaking and hearing kills the young men.
usage: When young men refuse the advice of an older man.
note: Repaired garbled English 'if he speak not' as 'speaking and hearing'.
igbo_raw: Áfp ngku ngBú okei; ekue näny neBu ikolo (As.).
english_raw: Seeing and keeping silence kills an old man; if he speak not hearing kills the young men. When young men refuse the advice of an older man.

igbo: Ọgọdọ abụghị enyi iyi.
english: A pond is not a companion of a river.
usage: If a young man tries to join his elders.
note: OCR 'Qgpdg' read as ọgọdọ; 'qbw'iyi' as enyi iyi.
igbo_raw: Qgpdg abuna qbw'iyi (0.0.).
english_raw: A pond is not a companion of a river. If a young man tries to join his elders.

igbo: Ọlịlị bọọ ọka, ọ na-ezo.
english: If ground squirrel digs up corn, he hides.
usage: When a young man acts in defiance of others.
note: OCR 'Ylili bob pka ozdé' read as Ọlịlị bọọ ọka, ọ na-ezo; bọọ uncertain.
igbo_raw: Ylili bob pka ozdé (I.A.).
english_raw: If ground squirrel digs up corn, he hides. When a young man acts in defiance of others.

igbo: Ka anya onye dị, ka ọ na-ahụ ụzọ.
english: As one's eyes are, so he sees the road.
usage: Young man should not raise laugh at meeting.
note: Thomas's 'ra' and 'ofy debe uzg' are normalized to dị and na-ahụ ụzọ.
igbo_raw: K' ainy' onye ra, k'ofy debe uzg (Uk.).
english_raw: As one's eyes are, so he sees the road. Young man should not raise laugh at meeting.

igbo: Maka mmiri na-ama Azọma, nwunye Ọba, oke nwoke na nwanyị isi ọba ga-ebinye.
english: Because the rain beats Azoma, wife of Oba, men's and women's heads Oba will cut off.
usage: There are old people in every town. Oba (the King of Benin) was young when his father died; all the wives but Azoma were carried off. The doctor told Oba to sacrifice her at the end of the street, to boil two hundred headpads and put them before the door, and to go to the ukbo and lie on his belly lamenting. At dawn Iyase came and asked why he lamented; he said the two hundred pads were for loads brought by Ezomo to hand over as his father's property. Iyase begged for forgiveness and all the property was returned. At the end of the year he built a house where Azoma was sacrificed, and men and women sacrificed annually. This story I found in a very similar form in Benin City.
note: The Igbo is heavily obscured by OCR and dialect spelling; the long explanatory story is retained in usage.
igbo_raw: Maka mili amwa Azgma, nwunye gba, ökei n'okporo K'pba gebenye (Ubul.).
english_raw: Because the rain beats Azoma, wife of Oba, man's and woman's heads oba will cut off. There are old people in every town (1). Qba (the King of Benin) was young when his father died; all the wives but Azoma were carried off. The doctor told Oba to sacrifice her at the end of the street, to boil two hundred headpads and put them before the door, and to go to the ukbo and lie on his belly lamenting. At dawn Ivase came and asked why he lamented; he said the two hundred pads were for loads brought by Ezomg to hand over as his father's property. Iyase begged for forgiveness and all the property was returned. At the end of the year he built a house where Azqma was sacrificed, and men and women sacrificed annually. This story I found in a very similar form in Benin City.

igbo: Ife adịghị edo ọka, ọ na-edo obodi.
english: The fool doubts what the wise man does not doubt.
usage: Old men are good counsellors.
note: 'obodi' is kept as Thomas's dialect word for fool; the second clause is restored from the English sense.
igbo_raw: Ife adedo oka çdo obodi (Ubul.).
english_raw: The fool doubts what the wise man does not doubt. Old men are good counsellors.

igbo: Agụ na-ebutere isi nkọ.
english: Old age brings baldness.
usage: To one who laughs at bald men.
note: 'Arp nte but' is read as Agụ na-ebutere, and 'ikpoco' as isi nkọ.
igbo_raw: Arp nte but' isí ikpoco (As.).
english_raw: Old age brings baldness. To one who laughs at bald men.

igbo: A naghị ebu ji egosi onye gwuru ya.
english: Yams are not taken to show the one who dug them.
usage: An outsider cannot explain to the owner what he has.
note: 'Adebuji' is normalized to A naghị ebu ji.
igbo_raw: Adebuji egosi onye gwue (Ubul.).
english_raw: Yams are not taken to show the one who dug them. An outsider cannot explain to the owner what he has.

igbo: Onye nwe ala ka ike.
english: One who rules the town is stronger.
usage: Strangers must lose the day.
note: 'ani' is normalized to ala.
igbo_raw: Onye nw' ani ka ike (0.0.).
english_raw: One who rules the town is stronger. Strangers must lose the day.

igbo: Ọ biakwa ka ọbịa bụ ohi nwa dị n'ala; afụ nene afụ nene bụ ohi otu mmiri.
english: The old thief comes as he came before; it is the first time when it's a strange thief.
usage: A stranger introduces a habit of theft.
note: The latter half of the proverb remains uncertain under the OCR damage.
igbo_raw: Qbiakwa K' obia b' ori nwadi ani; afunene afynene b' ori otu mili (Ubul.).
english_raw: The old thief comes as he came before; it is the first time when it's a strange thief. A stranger introduces a habit of theft.

igbo: Ọdịda adịghị ewufu ihe dị n'afọ; onye dara ebulu nke ya, bilie.
english: Falling does not throw away things in stomach; who falls takes up his and stands up.
usage: Strangers don't understand each other as friends do.
note: 'nisi pto' is unrecovered and restored as bilie from the sense; (Ada) is taken as a misreading of (Ala.).
igbo_raw: (Ada) Adada ewufu (si) ife di afo; onye dâda obulu nke
english_raw: nisi pto (I.A.). Falling does not throw away things in stomach; who falls takes up his and stands up. Strangers don't understand each other as friends do.

igbo: Iwe na nwa obu yi ọkọ, ebo adịghị eyi
english: Anger makes the child of obu wear oko cloth his ebo does not wear.
usage: If young men refuse and elders have to do work forbidden to them.
note: Restored 'rha' as 'na' and supplied the final 'eyi' from the sense.
igbo_raw: Iwe rha nwobu je okg ebowe adeji (0.0.).
english_raw: Anger makes the child of obu wear oko cloth his ebo does not wear. If young men refuse and elders have to do work forbidden to them.

igbo: Nwata bụ ọga, ọ bụrụ ọkụkọ; ọ bụrụ ewu, a họrọ oke nwoke
english: A child is a divider if it is a fowl; if it is a goat, they choose a grown man.
usage: When old men send young men to work, they don't send for them to share money.
note: 'rinne' is restored as 'nwoke' from Thomas's English 'man grown'.
igbo_raw: Nwata b'oga n'ob' okoko; obul' ewu warh' okei rinne
english_raw: (I.A.). Child is divider if it is fowl; if it is goat they chose a man grown. When old men send young men to work; they don't send for them to share money.

igbo: Adịghị ebe a na-egbu ene
english: They do not take a hunter's killing of a bush buck.
usage: If a new hand overthrows an old wrestler.
note: The OCR 'ebweni abwabu' is uncertain; the Igbo reading follows the English sense only loosely.
igbo_raw: Adeji ebweni abwabu ene (0.0.).
english_raw: They don't take hunter kill bush buck. If a new hand overthrows an old wrestler.

igbo: Okeleku adịghị akpa n'ụlọ okokporo
english: A lad does not collect in a bachelor's house.
note: 'okokbolo' is read as 'okokporo'; the verb 'collect' remains uncertain.
igbo_raw: Okeleku adiakpa n' ung okokbolo (As.).
english_raw: A lad does not (? collect) in a bachelor's house.

igbo: Iche iche ka ihe nni si agwụ
english: In different ways food utensils perish.
usage: Young and old are different.
note: OCR 'Ièg iõe' and 'grwu' are read as 'Iche iche' and 'agwụ' by the proverb's sense.
igbo_raw: Ièg iõe ka ifenni esi grwu (0.0.).
english_raw: In different ways food utensils perish. Young and old are different.

igbo: Ụdene tọọ ihe ọnụ, e were gbaba nye ya
english: A vulture touches a thing with his mouth; they cut and give him.
usage: If an older man comes to a palm wine drinker, he gets a big share.
note: 'gwaba' is read as 'gbaba' and 'nyeya' as 'nye ya'.
igbo_raw: Udeng to ife ony webe gwaba nyeya (Uk.).
english_raw: A vulture touches a thing with his mouth, they cut, give him. If an older man comes to a palm wine drinker he gets big share.

igbo: Mma jee ubi ropụta ji ise; ọ bụrụ na njọ jee, ncha ji dị ubi agwụ
english: Good went to the farm and dug five yams; if bad went, all the yams would have been finished.
usage: If young men all asked to speak in a meeting.
note: 'irujise' is uncertain, but the English 'five yams' fixes the reading as 'ji ise'.
igbo_raw: Mwa ej' ubwo robue irujise; obuluna njo je' nta ji di ubwo agwu (Uk.).
english_raw: Good went to farm and dug five yams; if bad went all the yams would have been finished. If young men all asked to speak in meeting.

igbo: Ọdịda amaghị oke
english: Falling does not know an old man.
igbo_raw: Ada adamwa okei (Uk.).
english_raw: Falling does not know old man.

igbo: Azị na-aṅụrị ọṅụ n'ụtụtọ; onweghị onye na-agba afa ihe ụwa ga-abụ n'anyasị.
english: The present generation rejoices in the morning; no one divines what the world will be in the evening.
usage: To careless young men.
note: OCR badly damaged; second clause reconstructed from Thomas's English.
igbo_raw: Azi nanwulo otôto; onwerg onye bwainye ainyase afa enu (Ala).
english_raw: The present generation rejoices in the morning; no one divines what the world will be in the evening. To careless young men.

igbo: Abụ m kwụ n'ụzọ na-akwadebe n'anyasị ụmụma dị n'ihu m.
english: One who has to start early prepares in the evening against dawn.
usage: A young man must not lose his opportunity.
note: First clause is a rough restoration of the damaged OCR; Thomas's syntax is uncertain.
igbo_raw: Abwakgm' 12g nakwadebe n'ainyase amgma di fu me
english_raw: (O.0.). One who has to start early prepares in the evening against dawn. A young man must not lose his opportunity.

igbo: Onye dị onye ka mara ihe.
english: One who is older than another knows more.
usage: To forward young men.
note: OCR 'mwa' read as 'mara'.
igbo_raw: Onye dig onye, ka mwa ife (0.0.).
english_raw: One who is older than another', knows more. To forward young men.

igbo: Ọkọrọ zọọ ụzọ akasị; ọ bụ enyi n'ọnọli.
english: Woman plants koko too early; she plants over spare ground (that her husband does not plant).
usage: Rebuke to a young man who tries to explain the case to the whole town instead of leaving it to the chief to do.
note: Proverb is obscure; only a rough orthographic restoration is possible.
igbo_raw: Okporo zok' yzo akasi ; obu enyi n'onoli (0.0.).
english_raw: Woman plants koko too early; she plants over spare ground (that her husband does not plant). Rebuke to a young man who tries to explain the case to the whole town instead of leaving it to the chief to do.

igbo: Nwata adaghị ije izizi akpọfe mmiri.
english: A child does not begin to walk and jump over a well.
usage: If young men speak without knowledge.
note: OCR 'adamwa' read as 'adaghị' and 'omi' as 'mmiri'.
igbo_raw: Nwata adamwa iïe izizi akbofe omi (0.0.).
english_raw: A child does not begin to walk and jump over a well. If young men speak without knowledge.

igbo: Nwata kwọọ aka, o soro ọgaranya rie nri.
english: A boy washes his hands and follows a rich man to eat.
usage: When a young man offers his opinion and it is approved by older men.
note: OCR 'osdlu ggalainya lienni' restored to 'o soro ọgaranya rie nri'.
igbo_raw: Nwata kwgie aka, osdlu ggalainya lienni (As.).
english_raw: A boy washes his hands and follows a rich man to eat. When a young man offers his opinion and it is approved by older men.

igbo: Ofili onye Oniọma, si ndị jekọ iyi zido ibu n'ala, ka ya bụ ala a na-agaghị aga.
english: Ofili of Oniomma tells those that go take inyi: put down loads on ground, that he is a country they never pass over.
usage: When the young men try to decide what old men should deal with.
note: Names and final clause are uncertain; 'inyi' may be 'iyi' (river).
igbo_raw: Ofili ony' Onigmma, si ndi jekg inyi zido ibu n'ani, kaiya by adagani Öca (As.).
english_raw: Ofili of Oniomma tells those that go take inyi: put down loads on ground, that he is a country they never pass over. When the young men try to decide what old men should deal with.

igbo: Agadi ka aka, ewebea nri.
english: When an old man gets too old, they give him less food.
usage: An old man cannot work like a young one.
note: Final clause is difficult; 'less food' may be Thomas's paraphrase.
igbo_raw: Agadi karhe, webenoa nnie (0.0.).
english_raw: When an old man gets too old, they give him less food. An old man cannot work like a young one.

igbo: Mmanya bara, ọzọ abịa.
english: Palm wine enters, noise comes.
usage: Names.
note: OCR 'Mwainya' = Mmanya, 'bàrhá' = bara, 'özó' = ọzọ, 'abia' = abịa.
igbo_raw: Mwainya bàrhá özó abia (I.A.).
english_raw: Palm wine enters, noise comes. Names.

igbo: Ene da
english: Look to the end.
usage: To one who talks without knowledge.
note: Thomas's 'Ené dà' likely 'Ene da'; the standard modern equivalent is uncertain.
igbo_raw: Ené dà (0.0.).
english_raw: Look to the end. To one who talks without knowledge.

igbo: Ụwa ra iwe.
english: Let the world leave off anger.
usage: When a poor man gets rich and his companions murmur.
note: 'Enu' likely ụwa; 'rha' = ra (leave).
igbo_raw: Enu rha iwe (0.0.).
english_raw: Let the world leave off anger. When a poor man gets rich and his companions murmur.

igbo: Asịa erue mụọ.
english: (Term of abuse) reaches the spirit.
usage: Sterile woman who bears a child after being abused and laughed at for sterility can name her child thus.
note: OCR 'eluemwg' = erue mụọ; 'mwo' in English = mụọ (spirit).
igbo_raw: Asia eluemwg (0.0.).
english_raw: (Term of abuse) reaches mwo. Sterile woman who bears a child after being abused and laughed at for sterility can name her child thus.

igbo: Anyị nọkwa ebe anyị nọ; anyị nọkwa ebe anyị na-eche gị.
english: We stay where we stay; we stay to wait for you.
usage: When a host says he has no more palm wine, his guests refuse to go and say this.
note: OCR heavily damaged; 'K'ainyi ng' read as ebe anyị nọ, 'budewe' as na-eche gị.
igbo_raw: Ainyi nokwa K'ainyi ng; ainyi nokwali budewe (As.).
english_raw: We stay where we stay; we stay to wait for you. When a host says he has no more palm wine, his guests refuse to go and say this.

igbo: Nwa nduru nwere ala; onye ntị nkụ asị, unu n'imara.
english: Child of dove has land; deaf man says, you know.
usage: At Ekwensu dance to people from other towns that they must give way.
note: OCR 'Nwanduli' = Nwa nduru, 'n'imwali' = n'imara (you know).
igbo_raw: Nwanduli nw'ani; onye nti nkpo asi, unu n'imwali
english_raw: (0.0.). Child of dove has land ; deaf man says, you know. At Ekwensu dance to people from other towns that they must give way.

igbo: Tụm bụ dozie.
english: Throw at me is an open place.
usage: When a man speaks in parables.
note: OCR 'bq' = bụ; 'dozi' uncertain, perhaps ọzara (open place).
igbo_raw: Tum bq dozi (I.A.).
english_raw: Throw at me is an open place. When a man speaks in perables.

igbo: Otu osisi dị n'ihu oba; ọ bọsị ọlụ akwụkwọ kọpụ.
english: One tree is in the yard of oba; the day it puts out leaves, they fall off.
note: OCR 'çzi' perhaps n'ihu (in front of); 'kobupu' = kọpụ/kpụpụ.
igbo_raw: Ofu osisi di çzi oba ; obosi olu akukwg kobupu (I.A.).
english_raw: One tree is in the yard of oba; the day it puts out leaves, they fall off.

igbo: Ejebe m ka m pụta, mee ka ha debe nye ife ọ ga-eli.
english: "I go and am coming back" makes people keep things for him to eat.
note: Restored OCR-damaged 'kamputa' as 'ka m pụta', 'fadebenye' as 'ha debe nye', and 'pgeli' as 'ọ ga-eli'.
igbo_raw: Ejebem kamputa me ka fadebenye ife pgeli (Ala).
english_raw: "I go and am coming back" makes people keep things for him to eat.

igbo: Aka dọọ igili, ka igili so.
english: Hand draws "bush rope," let igili follow.
usage: A man must come in reply to a message.
note: OCR 'gso' read as 'so'; 'do' restored as 'dọọ'.
igbo_raw: Aka do igili ka' igili gso (Uk.).
english_raw: Hand draws " bush rope," let igili follow. A man must come in reply to a message. F 2

igbo: Ngwa ngwa ka ha na-ala onye ekpenta.
english: Quickly they copulate a leper.
usage: By messenger, to hurry one he calls.
note: OCR 'Ngwargwa' read as 'Ngwa ngwa' and 'ekbente' as 'ekpenta'; English 'copulate' kept as Thomas's word.
igbo_raw: Ngwargwa ka wa ala onye ekbente (Ubul.).
english_raw: Quickly they copulate a leper. By messenger, to hurry one he calls.

igbo: Ọ bụghị sọ n'ọmụmụ ka nkịta na-aza okwu, ọ na-azazikwa nke na-amụghị nwa.
english: It is not only a fruitful woman that a dog answers; he answers one who is sterile.
usage: If a small man calls a meeting, or for help.
note: OCR badly damaged; reconstructed from English and known proverb shape.
igbo_raw: Qburg sp n'omumu ka nkita az okwu, nQzazikwa nkg
english_raw: agakpoa (I.A.). It is not only a fruitful woman that a dog answers, he auswers one who is sterile. If a small man calls a meeting, or for help.

igbo: Agụnkwo nwụrụ, ihe gburu ọkụkọ adịghị agwụ.
english: If the kite is dead, what kills fowl is not finished.
note: Restored 'Agunkwo' as 'Agụnkwo', 'gkoko' as 'ọkụkọ', and 'ádekagy' as 'adịghị agwụ'.
igbo_raw: Agunkwo nwuru, ife gbu gkoko ádekagy (Uk.).
english_raw: If kite is dead, what kills fowl is not finished.

igbo: Akwa dịkwa ebe Nesi kwere ya.
english: Cloth is where Nesi fixed it.
usage: If a man who calls a meeting is not ready to deal with the matter.
note: OCR 'Okg' read as 'Akwa', 'Neci' as 'Nesi', and 'kweme' as 'kwere ya'.
igbo_raw: Okg dikwa be Neci kweme (Ubul.).
english_raw: Cloth is where Neci fixed it. If man who calls meeting is not ready to deal with matter.

igbo: A na-ebu uzo, ọ nweghị mbana.
english: They never make a farm without a road.
usage: When no one replies in a meeting.
note: OCR garbled; reading is tentative, especially 'ubwo' and 'mbana'.

In Part III, page 194, of the present Report I dealt with the subject of tones and communicated the result of some tests. These tests were only roughly applied and in the light of further results, I feel some doubt as to how far they were accurate. As, however, my later enquiries dealt with the Asaba language, whereas the tests in question were applied to utterances of natives of Awka and Abg, it does not follow that the results of the latter were necessarily wrong. The main difference that appears is a much greater interval between the high tones and the low tones in Asaba. The low tones appear to have been accurately determined at C, but at Asaba the high tones appear to be at least five semi- tones above the previous datum. I am indebted for the results published here to my friend, who has worked over a number of phonograph records with me. The method adopted was as follows. In the case of single words the pitch was determined without any trouble by means of a tuning fork. This applies whether the tone was simple or compound. In the case of the sentences printed below the method was more complicated. I took charge of the phonograph and endeavoured to take the needle off at the end of the first syllable. When this was done with fair accuracy, it was possible to determine the pitch of the first syllable. The pitch of the second syllable was then determined in the same way, and so on until the end of the sentence was reached. Then, when the sentence was complete, the phonogram of it was repeated several times in order to get a connected impression of the variations of pitch and н 2 compare this with the results arrived at when the sounds were dealt with individually. I am also indebted to my friend, Dr. C. S. Myers, Lecturer in Experimental Psychology, Cambridge, for working over some of the records. In the main his results agree with those detailed here, though there is some difference of opinion as to certain intervals. The following table (Table I) shows the three tones found in monosyllables. From this it appears that the average high tone lies between B and By, the rising tone has an interval varying between six and twelve quarter tones, with an average of eight quarter tones, and the average rising tone is nearly Gib to BI. The falling tone has an interval vary- ing hetween fourteen and twenty quarter tones, with an average of nearly nineteen quarter tones, and is Gi# to Bg below. We may perhaps, however, regard these tones not as a simple case but as two distinet sets, for in the case of verbs the first component is Ab or G, whereas in the case of the demonstrative adjective wp the fall is from D to G. So far as monosyllables, therefore, are concerned, only three tones have been found. It must, however, be remem- bered that my phonograph records embrace only thirty-two words, whereas the total number of monosyllables, nine-tenths of which are verbs, is certainly over two hundred. There does not appear to be any simple low tone. A second record (618) was taken from another speaker, but, unfortunately, it was not sufficiently clear to give satisfactory results. The voice of this speaker, a boy of the same age as the first speaker, was distinctly lower. His high tone was about G, his rising tone from Ey to G, and his falling tone from Ely to G below, but there is only a single satisfactory example of each. His rising tone has an interval of six quarter tones, but the word was omitted from the other record and no comparison can be made with the other speaker. His falling tone is Ey to G below, which in the case of the other speaker was Ab to B below, a difference uf a semi-tone. A third speaker (Record 620a) showed considerable differences in certain words, but as he was reading from a written MS., these are probably simple errors. In other respects he agrees with the previous speakers; but shows a tendeney to make his high tone in monosyllables into a sharpened tone. If we now turn to dissyllables we find a different state of things. Cabove, A, G, C, G below, are all found in uncom- pounded tones. We cannot, however, at once assume that there is a corresponding number of simple tones in the language for mamy of these words are taken from sentences in which phrase tone possibly disguises word tone. In certain cases, however, such as gze, king, which as an individual word I had, independently of phonograph records, been disposed to regard as a two-four word, that is to say a word with the second tone on the first syllable and the fourth tone on the second syllable, the phonograph record shows that the actual pitch is E for the first syllable and G below for the second. If we take the àkwà, bed, which is usually regarded as having two low tones, but actually has a falling tone on the first syllable and a low tone on the second, we find that the low tone of the second is C. The question therefore arises whether the low tone of eze is the same as the low tone of akwa, and is only lowered on account of its position in the sentence, or whether we must distinguish a tone below C. The material at my disposal does not enable mne to say which solution is correct; but wg (this) has a falling tone to the same note. As regards the middle tones, a kwa, egg, is A and Ab, or, in an interrogative sentence, G and B; akwa, cloth, is G and A in an interrogative sentence or (GG#) and G_ in an affirma- tive one. In the absence of further material it hardly appears possible to reach any defimite conclusion on the subject of the number of the middle tones. If we assume that all the tones mentioned above are identical and that the C of the second syllable in àk wà is really a middle tone, the low tone being properly G, as in the second syllable of eze, we may then regard the middle tone as having a high component varying in pitch between F and A, and a low component varying in pitch between B and D. Or we may distinguish three middle tones, as is done in the subsequent tables., In addition to the above simple tones, a considerable variety of rising and falling tones is found in dissyllables. We find, for example, akwa, cloth, the first syllable being a rising tone G to G*, and the same tone is found in another case, gka, corn, has a rising tone G#to A, akam, I guess, and akam, I am bigger, then have rising tones, Fto G, in the first syllable, with only a semi-tone or a tone interval between the components. This appears to be entirely different from the rising tone in the monosyllables, where in only four out of thirteen cases was the interval so small as a tone and a half as shown above (see Table III). I term the small rises (or falls) sharpened (or flattened) tones. If we now turn to falling tones, we find a small fall from D to C in the first syllable of äkwà, bed, in interrogative sentences; and in affirmative sentences the fall is from E to ©; in the second syllable of ago, leopard, the fall is from A to G#. Although the interval is the same as the first one, it does not seem possible to regard these two falling tones as identical; in the first two cases the fall is from four to six quarter tones. We may, perhaps provisionally say that there is a falling tone lying between E and C, and a flattened tone hetween A and Gt. So far as can be seen from a small number of instances, neither of these tones corresponds to those shown in Table III, which are found in monosyllables. It may, however, be repeated that the number of instances is exceedingly small; in the case of the demonstrative adjective, w,o, the example was taken from a sentence, and the pitch may, therefore, have been influenced by phrase tone. At the same time it may be remarked that the falling tone in wp is almost identical with the two tones found in the word gze. It is, therefore, by no means so evident that the two tones found in monosyllables are identical, especially as in the one case the interval is fourteen quarter tones, whereas in the verbs in two cases out of three the interval is a tone and a half greater.
